explanation: In a many-to-many design, the association table stores a foreign key to each related table so each row represents one project-team-member pairing. Those two columns must also be constrained so the same pairing is not stored repeatedly. That uniqueness can be enforced by making the two foreign keys a composite primary key or by using a surrogate key and still requiring the pair to be unique. The other choices fail because they omit one side of the relationship or ignore the need for keys altogether.

Option A correctly joins books to author_book on book_id and then filters the linking rows to author_id = 7. Option B incorrectly tries to join authors directly to books, but those tables are not directly related in the schema. Option C treats 7 as a book_id rather than an author_id. Option D returns author names, not book titles, and also uses the wrong direct join pattern.

options.text: SELECT b.title FROM books b JOIN author_book ab ON b.book_id = ab.book_id WHERE ab.author_id = 7;
SELECT b.title FROM books b JOIN authors a ON b.book_id = a.author_id WHERE a.author_id = 7;
SELECT title FROM books WHERE book_id = 7;
SELECT a.name FROM authors a JOIN books b ON a.author_id = b.book_id WHERE a.author_id = 7;

prompt: A database has tables authors(author_id, name), books(book_id, title), and author_book(author_id, book_id). Each row in author_book links one author to one book. Which query correctly returns the titles of books written by author_id = 7?

explanation: A is correct because this is a weak/composite identifier pattern. The attempt exists only in the context of a candidate taking an exam, so candidate_id and exam_id identify the parent relationship, and attempt_no acts as a local discriminator that is unique within that candidate-exam pair. Together, candidate_id + exam_id + attempt_no uniquely identify each attempt. B fails because candidate_id + exam_id cannot distinguish multiple attempts for the same pair. C fails because attempt_no is not unique across all candidates for an exam. D denormalizes repeating attempt data into one column instead of representing each attempt as its own row.

options.text: Use an attempt table with candidate_id, exam_id, and attempt_no as a composite identifier
Use candidate_id and exam_id as the identifier, because they already identify the candidate-exam relationship
Use exam_id and attempt_no as the identifier, because attempt numbers are tied to exams
Use a person table column that lists all exam attempts for each candidate
